1.pericope_label: Hear this word that the Lord hath spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying, You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.

schools.summary: Settle the shape of the book from the repeated call to hear, and weigh whether children or house of Israel is the better reading; make the intimacy the ground of chastisement rather than its measure.
Read the knowing as distinguishing love and the therefore as reproach, God bringing forward his benefits to enhance the ingratitude.
Make the inference proportional, the punishment answering to the privileges enjoyed and the grace abused.
Casts the summons as an indictment read to a prisoner at the bar, who must consider what answer he will make.

debates.question: What does therefore mean after you only have I known?

positions.position: The punishment shall answer to the privileges enjoyed and the grace abused.
Chosen as peculiar ones and therefore judged for abusing these mercies.
More probably the intimacy is the ground of gracious chastisement, since to go on in sin without rebuke is the greatest curse that can befall a nation or a man.
Not a concession to what they boasted of but a reproach, God bringing forward his benefits to enhance the sin of a people returning the worst recompense.
The knowing is distinguishing love rather than bare omniscience, none having been known with this affection or these favours.
Both kingdoms, in the phrase the whole family, though the northern is chiefly in the prophet's mind; children of Israel is unusual here and many manuscripts substitute house of Israel.
The twelve tribes at the opening and the northern kingdom afterwards.
Not the ten tribes only but Judah, since it is spoken against the whole family brought up out of Egypt.

outliers.claim: Uses the repeated call to hear to settle the structure of the book: three successive chapters open with it, but they are not three separate sermons, rather the leading thoughts of spoken appeals grouped into one long admonition to repentance.

themes: Hear this word that the Lord hath spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying,
You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.

3.pericope_label: Can two walk together, except they be agreed? Will a lion roar in the forest, when he hath no prey? will a young lion cry out of his den, if he have taken nothing? Can a bird fall in a snare upon the earth, where no gin is for him? shall one take up a snare from the earth, and have taken nothing at all?

schools.summary: Canvass the candidates for the two walkers and settle on God and Israel; correct the snare clause and apply it to armies already in motion.
Reduce the accumulated similitudes to five particulars, chief among them that nothing happens by chance.
Turn the first question into direct address in the divine person, and reconstruct the mechanism of the trap.

debates.question: Who are the two that walk together?

positions.position: God and Israel, on the authority of four commentators against two other proposals, since obedience and communion of heart are what scripture calls walking with God.
The plain case first, that two cannot walk together without agreement of road and affection; without friendship no fellowship and without concord no communion.
God and the people, put as direct address: while you loved and served me I walked among you, but now our natures are opposite.
Can you have God's presence while you walk so contrary to him?
Providence, since a bird is never taken without a snare set by the fowler's design and God's will.
The same, with the reason men miss it: calamity comes unexpectedly and is ascribed to chance, but nets do not weave themselves.
Read rather does the snare rise up from the ground and take nothing at all; Israel like a silly dove is falling into snares already springing from the earth.

outliers.claim: Calls the snare clause curious and deserving further consideration, and reconstructs the mechanism as a spring trap of the kind used for vermin, whose jaws open backward and press on a spring held by a key.

themes: Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Will a lion roar in the forest, when he hath no prey? will a young lion cry out of his den, if he have taken nothing?
Can a bird fall in a snare upon the earth, where no gin is for him? shall one take up a snare from the earth, and have taken nothing at all?

6.pericope_label: Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? shall there be evil in a city, and the Lord hath not done it? Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets. The lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord God hath spoken, who can but prophesy?

schools.summary: Refers the lion's roar back to the opening of the book and finds the voice of the Lord so clearly portending judgment that universal terror follows.
Turns the trumpet into a reproach for torpor, and makes the warning of the prophets a privilege Israel had over the heathen nations.
Restrict the word evil to punishment rather than moral evil, and propose that the closing verb means to supplicate rather than to proclaim.

debates.question: What does who can but prophesy mean?

positions.position: The verb should be taken in its natural signification, to pray or deprecate vengeance: who can help supplicating mercy that the judgment may be averted?
The prophet cannot but speak what he has heard.
A reproof of the hearers' habit of contending with the prophets, asking what these men intend and why they will not let us rest.
The voice of the Lord is so audible that universal terror inevitably follows.
Spoken from the prophet's own experience as a herdsman who had often heard a lion roar.

outliers.claim: Makes the revelation to the prophets a comparative privilege: other nations God punished without warning, summoning neither Edomites nor Ammonites nor Egyptians, but Israel he preceded with his word, so every excuse was taken away.
Guards the clause about evil in a city: God does it by his own hand or by those he employs, and whoever the instruments, he is the principal agent.

themes: Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? shall there be evil in a city, and the Lord hath not done it?
Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
The lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord God hath spoken, who can but prophesy?

9.pericope_label: Publish in the palaces at Ashdod, and in the palaces in the land of Egypt, and say, Assemble yourselves upon the mountains of Samaria, and behold the great tumults in the midst thereof, and the oppressed in the midst thereof. For they know not to do right, saith the Lord, who store up violence and robbery in their palaces. Therefore thus saith the Lord God; An adversary there shall be even round about the land; and he shall bring down thy strength from thee, and thy palaces shall be spoiled.

schools.summary: Correct the preposition to on the palaces, place the observers on the high ground, and state the moral charge in its severest form as a dead conscience.
Read the summons as the appointment of foreign judges over a people who would not submit to God's own tribunal.
Take the publication from the housetops and read the encirclement as a sentence: wherever they turn they shall meet a foe.
Frames the summons as public notice given to inquisitive neighbours who are conversant with the public intelligence.

debates.question: What does it mean that they know not to do right?

positions.position: They had lost the practical knowledge of justice by long use of unjust ways, knowing what was right in theory but not in practice.
There are none so blind as those who will not see, their eyes closed by themselves.
Not merely lost perception but indifferent to the distinction: utter moral impotence, a dead conscience, the light within them darkness.
Wilful blindness; they had cast away everything just and sinned without shame, brute animals void of judgment.
The Assyrian, though not named; adversary is to be preferred to the affliction of two ancient versions.
The Assyrian, besetting the whole land as one besieged city.
A foe met wherever they turn, with no escape.
An enemy besieging on every side, the noun not being a verb in the imperative as some propose.

outliers.claim: States the causal link the passage makes, that the violence and robbery stored up in the palaces are what bring about the ruin of the kingdom.

themes: Publish in the palaces at Ashdod, and in the palaces in the land of Egypt, and say, Assemble yourselves upon the mountains of Samaria, and behold the great tumults in the midst thereof, and the oppressed in the midst thereof.
For they know not to do right, saith the Lord, who store up violence and robbery in their palaces.
Therefore thus saith the Lord God; An adversary there shall be even round about the land; and he shall bring down thy strength from thee, and thy palaces shall be spoiled.

12.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; As the shepherd taketh out of the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear; so shall the children of Israel be taken out that dwell in Samaria in the corner of a bed, and in Damascus in a couch. Hear ye, and testify in the house of Jacob, saith the Lord God, the God of hosts, That in the day that I shall visit the transgressions of Israel upon him I will also visit the altars of Beth–el: and the horns of the altar shall be cut off, and fall to the ground. And I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Correct the verb to delivereth, take the shanks and ear-pieces for the surviving remnant, and admit that whether two houses or two chambers are meant is uncertain.
Deny that the surviving remnant mitigates the sentence, and read the palaces as a rebuke of confidence in wealth.
Supply the historical fulfilment at the altars and a traveller's illustration of the summer houses.

debates.question: Who is told to hear and testify?

positions.position: The prophets and priests, whose business was to admonish the people of their danger.
The prophets.
The foreign nations summoned a few verses earlier.

debates.question: What are the winter and summer houses?

positions.position: Either two dwellings, town and country, or two parlours in one house; the threat reaches city and country alike.
Uncertain whether two classes of royal abode or different chambers of one house, the parallels admitting either.
Both the poor habitations of the country and the lofty palaces of the fortified cities, with country seats like those around a North African city.
The winter house in the chief city and the summer houses as places of pleasure.
A paraphrase designating the palaces, since the poor are content with one cottage for both seasons.

outliers.claim: Reads the fresh introduction before the altars as a deliberate device, bringing that feature of the threat into peculiar prominence.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; As the shepherd taketh out of the mouth of the lion two legs, or a piece of an ear; so shall the children of Israel be taken out that dwell in Samaria in the corner of a bed, and in Damascus in a couch.
Hear ye, and testify in the house of Jacob, saith the Lord God, the God of hosts,
That in the day that I shall visit the transgressions of Israel upon him I will also visit the altars of Beth–el: and the horns of the altar shall be cut off, and fall to the ground.
And I will smite the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish, and the great houses shall have an end, saith the Lord.
